Updates in Version 2.2026 of the NCCN Guidelines for Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation:

MS-1
• The Discussion section has been updated to reflect the changes in the algorithm. 

Updates in Version 1.2026 of the NCCN Guidelines for Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation:
General
• Page HCT-5 has been removed from the algorithm. The content from this page has been modified and added to HCT-A 1 of 11 and HCT-C.
HCT-2
• Pre-Transplant Recipient Evaluation
Clinical Assessment

 ◊Sub-bullet modified/moved from HCT-3 and added to this page: Discuss fertility preservation for individuals of childbearing potential
 ◊Sub-bullet added: Consider geriatric assessment or HCT specific risk assessment tool for older adults as indicated per institutional preference
Imaging

 ◊Sub-bullet modified: Donor and recipient short tandem repeat (STR) genotyping to inform post-transplant chimerism analysis (for allogeneic HCT)
HCT-A 1 of 11
• Principles of Conditioning for Hematopoietic Cell Transplant 
General Principles added: 

 ◊Conditioning for allogeneic transplant is based on disease, recipient age/comorbidities, graft source, and degree of HLA disparity.
 ◊Conditioning for autologous transplant is based on disease and recipient age/comorbidities. 
Definitions of Conditioning Regimen Intensity

 ◊Busulfan, sub-bullets added: 

 
– Pharmacokinetic (PK) monitoring is required for oral busulfan and is preferred for IV busulfan, as underexposure has been associated with 

relapse and reduced overall survival, while overexposure is associated with increased risk for toxicity such as veno-occlusive disease (VOD)/
sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) and increased non-relapse mortality (NRM).
 
– Optimal busulfan exposure targets for all conditioning regimens remain undefined due to the absence of prospective randomized trials; however, 

most recommendations fall within 60–100 mg x h/L as the proposed total area under the curve (AUC) target. Busulfan AUC targeting should only 
be performed by centers with expertise in this area.
HCT-A 3 of 11
• Bullet 1 modified: This list is not comprehensive. Other options can be considered. Please refer to references for contextual information and further 
details on dosing recommendations.
MA Regimens - Allogeneic Transplant

 ◊Fludarabine + TBI, regimen and dosing revised: 

 
– Fludarabine 30 mg/m2/day for 4 3 Days

 
– TBI 12–13.2 Gy fractionated

 
– OR

 
– Fludarabine 30 mg/m2/day for 4 Days

 
– TBI 8–12 Gy fractionated
 ◊Footnote d added: Risks and benefits should be weighed carefully when making dosing decisions for fludarabine and TBI, including consideration of 

relapse risk, regimen-related toxicity, and patient comorbidities.

Continued

UPDATES

pages.text:
Updates in Version 1.2026 of the NCCN Guidelines for Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation:

GVHD-E 2 of 4
• Footnote e added: Remestemcel-L-rknd has shown promising results in the pediatric population and studies are ongoing in adults. Remestemcel-L-rknd 
is currently FDA approved for the treatment of steroid-refractory acute GVHD in pediatric patients ≥2 months.
GVHD-E 3 of 4
• Reference added: Kurtzberg J, Abdel-Azim H, Carpenter P, et al. A phase 3, single-arm, prospective study of remestemcel-l, ex vivo culture-expanded 
adult human mesenchymal stromal cells for the treatment of pediatric patients who failed to respond to steroid treatment for acute graft-versus-host 
disease. Biol Blood Marrow Transplant 2020;26:845-854.
GVHD-F 1 of 2
• GVHD Supportive Care
All Patients, bullet 2, sub-bullet 4 revised: ....such as in recipients of a UCB transplant, in children undergoing transplantation for inherited or acquired 

disorders associated with B-cell deficiency, and in patients with chronic GVHD with recurrent sinopulmonary infections.
Chronic GVHD

 ◊Bullet 1, sub-bullet 1 revised: Sialagogues (eg, cevimeline) may be considered with severe xerostomia.
 ◊Bullet 2, sub-bullet 2 revised: Patients may benefit from artificial tears, topical immunosuppressants, autologous serum drops, punctal plugs, or gas-

permeable scleral lenses.
 ◊Bullet 2, sub-bullet 3 revised: Patients with severe ocular sicca may benefit from cholinergic agents (cevimeline or pilocarpine).
 ◊Bullet 5 modified: Physical therapy may help patients with musculoskeletal, sclerotic, or neuromuscular disease. Muscle relaxants and/or anti-

spasmodics may be considered for patients with muscle cramps.

UPDATES

INTRODUCTION

The NCCN Guidelines for Hematopoietic Cell 
Transplantation (HCT) pertain to the care of adult patients 

undergoing HCT for malignant diseases.

PRE-TRANSPLANT RECIPIENT EVALUATIONa,b
ADDITIONAL EVALUATION AS CLINICALLY INDICATED

As clinically indicated:
• Additional Clinical Assessment
Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis
Pregnancy test for individuals of childbearing potential
Physical therapy evaluation (strength, flexibility, function)
Nutritional evaluation
Consider geriatric assessment for select patients (category 2B) 

(See NCCN Guidelines for Older Adult Oncology)
Dental evaluation (for allogeneic HCT)
• Additional Imaging
CT (chest and/or sinuses)
• Additional Laboratory Tests
Epstein-Barr virus testing or other infectious disease testing 

(if high risk) (eg, tuberculosis, strongyloides, human T-cell 
lymphotropic virus types I and II [for allogeneic HCT])
HLA antibody assessment if using HLA-mismatched donor 
24-hour urine creatinine clearance (for borderline renal 

dysfunction or low muscle mass)
Urine toxicology screen if history of substance use disorder
Thyroid-stimulating hormone level
Iron profile (including ferritin level)
Blood lipid panel
Vitamin D level

HEMATOPOIETIC CELL MOBILIZATION REGIMENSr

Allogeneic Donors

Autologous Donors
Filgrastims ± Plerixafor
• Filgrastim: 10 mcg/kg weight SC for 4–5 Days 
Continued daily until collection goal is met
• Plerixafor: 0.24 mg/kg actual body weight SC (max 40 mg/day) on the day before apheresist

Filgrastims
• 10 mcg/kg donor weight SC (or split twice daily)
• Daily for 4–5 Days
• Collect on Day 4 or 5

Filgrastims + Cyclophosphamide ± Plerixafor
• Cyclophosphamide: 1500–3000 mg/m2 IV
• Filgrastim: 10 mcg/kg SC
Daily starting 24 Hours after cyclophosphamide and continuing until collection goal is met. 

Begin apheresis at least 4–5 Days after cyclophosphamide administration.u 
• Plerixafor: 0.24 mg/kg actual body weight SC (max 40 mg/day) on the day before apheresist

Sargramostim + Cyclophosphamide ± Plerixafor
• Cyclophosphamide: 1500–3000 mg/m2 IV
• Sargramostim: 250 mcg/m2/day SC
IV over 24 Hours or SC once daily
Daily starting 24 Hours after cyclophosphamide and continuing until collection goal is met. 

Begin apheresis at least 4–5 Days after cyclophosphamide administration.u
• Plerixafor: 0.24 mg/kg actual body weight SC (max 40 mg/day) on the day before apheresist

Pegfilgrastim + Plerixafor
• Pegfilgrastim: 6 mg SC on Day 1 
• Upfront plerixafor 0.24 mg/kg actual body weight SC (max 40 mg/day) on Day 3 followed by 
apheresis on Day 4 

Filgrastims + Motixafortide
• Filgrastim: 10 mcg/kg SC daily x 4 Days prior to first dose of motixafortide
• Motixafortide: 1.25 mg/kg actual body weight SC 10–14 Hours prior to initiation of apheresis 

r An FDA-approved biosimilar is an appropriate substitute for any recommended systemic biologic therapy in the NCCN Guidelines.
s Tbo-filgrastim or an FDA-approved biosimilar is an appropriate substitute for filgrastim.
t Plerixafor is generally administered 11 hours prior to stem cell collection. 
u Consider checking circulating CD34+ cells and initiating apheresis based on institutional guidelines.

footnotes.r: An FDA-approved biosimilar is an appropriate substitute for any recommended systemic biologic therapy in the NCCN Guidelines.
footnotes.s: Tbo-filgrastim or an FDA-approved biosimilar is an appropriate substitute for filgrastim.

PRINCIPLES OF CONDITIONING FOR HEMATOPOIETIC CELL TRANSPLANT

General Principles
• Conditioning for allogeneic transplant is based on disease, recipient age/comorbidities, graft source, and degree of HLA disparity.
• Conditioning for autologous transplant is based on disease and recipient age/comorbidities. 
• Indications for HCT vary by disease. Refer to applicable NCCN Guidelines for Treatment by Cancer Type.

Definitions of Conditioning Regimen Intensity1
• Myeloablative (MA) conditioning regimen: One that will cause irreversible (or close to irreversible) pancytopenia. Hematopoietic cell support is required 
to rescue marrow function and prevent aplasia-related death. Examples include: 
Total body irradiation (TBI) ≥5 Gy single dose or ≥8 Gy fractionated
Busulfan >8 mg/kg orally (>6.4 mg/kg IV) or busulfan plasma exposure unit equivalenta

 ◊Pharmacokinetic (PK) monitoring is required for oral busulfan and is preferred for IV busulfan, as underexposure has been associated with relapse 

and reduced overall survival, while overexposure is associated with increased risk for toxicity such as veno-occlusive disease (VOD)/sinusoidal 
obstruction syndrome (SOS) and increased non-relapse mortality (NRM).2-4

 
– Optimal busulfan exposure targets for all conditioning regimens remain undefined due to the absence of prospective randomized trials; however, 

most recommendations fall within 60–100 mg x h/L as the proposed total area under the curve (AUC) target.a Busulfan AUC targeting should only 
be performed by centers with expertise in this area.5-7
• Non-myeloablative (NMA) conditioning regimen: One that will produce minimal cytopenia, and there is no absolute need for hematopoietic cell support. 
Examples include:
TBI ≤2 Gy ± purine analog
Total lymphoid irradiation + antithymocyte globulin (ATG)
• Reduced-intensity conditioning (RIC) regimen: One that does not fulfill criteria for MA or NMA.

a Busulfan plasma exposure unit should be reported as AUC in mg x h/L. For example, AUC 5000 µM x min is equivalent to 20.5 mg x h/L (McCune JS, et al. Biol Blood 

Marrow Transplant 2019;25:1890-1897).

pages.text:
PRINCIPLES OF CONDITIONING FOR HEMATOPOIETIC CELL TRANSPLANT

Special Situations
• For patients with significant pulmonary dysfunction, caution is 
recommended if using high-dose (HD) busulfan, carmustine, and HD 
TBI. 
• Increased risk of VOD/SOS has been associated with the use of:
HD busulfan and HD TBI in patients with significant liver dysfunction. 
Dual alkylator-based regimens with pre-transplant inotuzumab or 

gemtuzumab. 
• The combination of sirolimus9,10 and tacrolimus may be associated with 
higher risk of VOD/SOS and thrombotic microangiopathy, especially if 
used with MA regimens.11-16

• Increased risk of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) has been associated 
with patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (pre- or post-
HCT) and mogamulizumab. 
Consider a minimum 8- to 12-week window between these treatments 

and the start of transplant conditioning if clinically feasible.13-16

• Thiotepa can be excreted through the skin and requires special skin 
care. Refer to the package insert. 

Allogeneic Conditioning Regimen Selection
• The choice among an MA, NMA, or RIC regimen is a nuanced 
decision that should be made by the transplant team at the time of 
patient evaluation or upon review of pre-transplant organ testing, 
frailty/geriatric assessment, or other evaluation.
• Conditioning regimen intensity depends on:
Patient age (chronologic and physiologic)
Performance status
HCT-CI and other pertinent comorbiditiesb
Disease type
Remission status (including measurable residual disease)
History of prior HCT
• MA regimens may be preferred for the following disease types, if 
the patient is young and fitb,8:
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (TBI-based regimens preferred)
Acute myeloid leukemia
Chronic myeloid leukemia
Myelodysplastic syndromes
• RIC/NMA regimens may be preferred for:
Lymphoma (non-Hodgkin lymphoma [NHL] or Hodgkin lymphoma 

[HL])
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
Plasma cell disorders (eg, multiple myeloma, plasma cell 

leukemia)
Patients who have received a prior autologous HCT
Patients who are older or unfitb

b The HCT-CI predicts the risk of NRM after transplant more accurately than age and performance status; however, it does not predict the risk of relapse. Detailed 

explanation of the HCT-CI has been published (Sorror ML. Blood 2013;121:2854-2863). See HCT-CI score calculator: http://hctci.org. 

References

PRINCIPLES OF CONDITIONING FOR HEMATOPOIETIC CELL TRANSPLANT

Suggested Doses/Modifications by Weight76

Busulfanq,2,3
• Adults: mg/kg dosing: dose based on 25% adjusted body weight 
Body surface area (BSA) dosing: dose based on total body weight 
• Risk of VOD/SOS is correlated with higher busulfan exposure (higher AUC)
Carmustine
• Dose adults on BSA 
• Total body weight ≤120% ideal body weight: dose based on total body weight 
• Total body weight >120% ideal body weight: dose based on 25% adjusted body weight 
• Pulmonary toxicity >50% at 600 mg/m2 with multiple agent regimens. Maximum tolerated dose of 1200 mg/m2 as 
single agent with 9.5% pulmonary toxicity
Cyclophosphamide
• Cy200 regimen: dose based on the lesser of total body weight or ideal body weight
• Cy120 regimen: dosing can be either ideal body weight or total body weight until >120% ideal body weight, then 
dose based on 25% adjusted body weightr 
Cytarabine
Dose adults on BSA based on total body weight
Etoposide
• Mg/kg dosing: dose based on 25% adjusted body weightr 
• BSA dosing: dose based on total body weight
Fludarabine
Dose adults on BSA based on total body weight
Melphalan
• Dose adults on BSA based on total body weight 
Thiotepa
• Dose adults on BSA if total body weight ≤120%
• Total body weight ≤120% ideal body weight dose on BSA based on total body weight
• Total body weight >120% ideal body weight dose on BSA based on 40% adjusted body weightr

Treosulfan
Dose adults on BSA based on total body weight 

q PK monitoring is required for oral busulfan and is preferred for IV busulfan.
r 25% adjusted body weight indicates ideal body weight + 0.25 (total body weight - ideal body weight); 40% adjusted body weight indicates ideal body weight + 0.4 (total 

body weight - ideal body weight).

PRINCIPLES OF GVHD PROPHYLAXIS

FOOTNOTES

a The following is a non-inclusive list of GVHD prophylaxis regimens. However, these are the most commonly used regimens among the NCCN Member Institutions. The 

selection of regimens should be based on institutional preferences, physician experience, and patient-specific factors. Please refer to corresponding published data for 
dosing recommendations (HCT-B 4 of 6).
b This recommendation is based on randomized phase II data.
c There is no benefit to adding prednisone to cyclosporine + MTX (Chao NJ, et al. Biol Blood Marrow Transplant 2000;6:254-261; Ross M, et al. Biol Blood Marrow 

Transplant 1999;5:285-291).
d Applies to HLA-matched unrelated donor HCT. 
e In the appropriate setting, both ATG and alemtuzumab can be paired with either RIC or MAC.
f Reconstitution of CD34-selected cells requires MAC and ATG-based conditioning to support engraftment. See Discussion for specific MAC regimens studied in this 

setting. This approach may be considered for patients ineligible for myeloablative HCT (age, comorbidity) who would benefit from MAC with respect to reducing the risk 
of relapse. The potential excess toxicity associated with MAC may be offset by the absence of MTX/CNI-related toxicity (Shah GL, et al. Biol Blood Marrow Transplant 
2018;24:142-149).
g CD34 selection utilizing an FDA-approved reagent system may be considered for patients with AML who have achieved first morphologic complete remission who have 

an HLA-identical sibling donor and are following a myeloablative conditioning regimen. 
h Ex vivo CD3+/CD19+ depleted allografts from haploidentical donors have been performed using RIC. (Sestili S, et al. Cancer 2018;124:2142-2150; Federmann B, et 

al. Haematologica 2012;97:1523-1531; Bethge WA, et al. Blood Cells Mol Dis 2008;40:13-19; Bethge WA, et al. Bone Marrow Transplant 2022;57:423-430; Prezioso L, 
et al. Bone Marrow Transplant 2019;54:698-702). 
i Indicated for single allele mismatched donors (7/8).

References

pages.title: Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation
pages.text:
PRINCIPLES OF GVHD PROPHYLAXIS

Additional GVHD Prophylaxis Considerations Based on Conditioning Intensity: 
• CNI plus MTX remains one of the standard approaches in HLA-matched donor HCTs, especially in the setting of MAC conditioning. In RIC peripheral 
blood progenitor cell (PBSC) transplantation, the CTN1703 trial demonstrated superior 1-year GVHD-free, relapse-free survival with PTCy compared to 
tacrolimus + MTX.2 Evaluation of long-term survival outcomes (beyond 1 year) is awaited. 
• In HLA-mismatched unrelated donor HCTs, robust data exist supporting the use of PTCy-based prophylaxis. Abatacept has also been shown effective 
in combination with CNI-MTX. In the setting of non-myeloablative conditioning with Flu/TBI 200–300 cGy, the triple regimen of MMF/CSA/sirolimus was 
superior to the historical CSA/MMF.56 In addition, in a more recent phase III study, PTCy/CSA/sirolimus was superior to MMF/CSA/sirolimus.8
• For umbilical cord blood transplant, CNI plus MMF remains the standard/most experienced approach. 
• Data on ex-vivo CD34 selection/T cell depletion are largely based on MAC.
• Abatacept is FDA-approved in combination with CNI and MTX backbone for aGVHD prophylaxis in MUD and 1 allele mismatched MMUD 
transplantation with both MAC and RIC conditioning based on results from the ABA2 study.15 Addition of abatacept to the CNI/MTX backbone provides 
modest benefit without added toxicities for MUD and represents an alternative to PTCy for 7/8 MMUD.23

pages.text:
POST-TRANSPLANT FOLLOW-UP

• Monitoring for post-transplant complications such as:
Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) (for allogeneic transplant), see Diagnosis/Workup of GVHD (GVHD-1)
Infections (See NCCN Guidelines for Prevention and Treatment of Cancer-Related Infections)
Multi-organ dysfunctiona
Monitoring for graft rejection/failure per institutional preference
Monitoring for disease relapse is recommended for all patients who have undergone HCT.
• Intensive supportive care is required for all post-transplant recipients. For GVHD Supportive Care, see GVHD-F.

a Potential post-transplant organ toxicities are too numerous to list but can include cardiac, pulmonary, renal, and/or liver complications. Hepatic VOD/SOS is one 

potentially life-threatening complication. Defibrotide is FDA approved for the treatment of hepatic VOD/SOS in patients with renal or pulmonary dysfunction following 
HCT based on non-randomized trials. See defibrotide prescribing information for further details.

SUGGESTED SYSTEMIC AGENTS FOR STEROID-REFRACTORY GVHD

• Participation in clinical trials is encouraged.
• The following systemic agents are used in conjunction with corticosteroids for steroid-refractory GVHD. There is insufficient evidence to recommend one 
systemic agent as preferred over another. However, these are the most commonly used agents among the NCCN Member Institutions. 
• The selection of systemic agent should be based on institutional preferences, physician experience, agent's toxicity profile, the effect of prior treatment, 
drug interactions, convenience/accessibility, and patient tolerability.

pages.text:
SUGGESTED SYSTEMIC AGENTS FOR STEROID-REFRACTORY GVHD

FOOTNOTES

a For patients receiving immunosuppressive agents for GVHD, see NCCN Guidelines for Prevention and Treatment of Cancer-Related Infections. 
b An FDA-approved biosimilar is an appropriate substitute for any recommended systemic biologic therapy in the NCCN Guidelines.
c Ruxolitinib is FDA approved for the treatment of adult and pediatric patients (age ≥12 years) with either steroid-refractory acute GVHD, or chronic GVHD after failure of 

one or two lines of systemic therapy.
d Psoralen and ultraviolet A irradiation (PUVA) may be used for sclerotic or cutaneous GVHD if ECP is not available or feasible. 
e Remestemcel-L-rknd has shown promising results in the pediatric population and studies are ongoing in adults. Remestemcel-L-rknd is currently FDA approved for the 

treatment of steroid-refractory acute GVHD in pediatric patients ≥2 months. 
f Ibrutinib is FDA approved for the treatment of adult and pediatric patients ≥1 year with chronic GVHD after failure of one or more lines of systemic therapy. Ibrutinib 

should be used with caution in patients with a history of heart arrhythmias or heightened risk of bleeding.
g Belumosudil is FDA approved for the treatment of adult and pediatric patients (age ≥12 years) with chronic GVHD after failure of two or more prior lines of systemic 

therapy. 
h Axatilimab-csfr is FDA approved for the treatment of adult and pediatric patients weighing ≥40 kg with chronic GVHD after failure of at least two prior lines of systemic 

therapy.

NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
Category 1
Based upon high-level evidence (≥1 randomized phase 3 trials or high-quality, robust meta-analyses), there is 
uniform NCCN consensus (≥85% support of the Panel) that the intervention is appropriate.
Category 2A
Based upon lower-level evidence, there is uniform NCCN consensus (≥85% support of the Panel) that the 
intervention is appropriate.
Category 2B
Based upon lower-level evidence, there is NCCN consensus (≥50%, but <85% support of the Panel) that the 
intervention is appropriate.
Category 3
Based upon any level of evidence, there is major NCCN disagreement that the intervention is appropriate. 
All recommendations are category 2A unless otherwise indicated.

NCCN Categories of Preference

Preferred
Interventions that are based on superior efficacy, safety, and evidence; and, when appropriate, 
affordability.

Other recommended
Other interventions that may be somewhat less efficacious, more toxic, or based on less mature data; 
or significantly less affordable for similar outcomes.

Useful in certain 
circumstances
Other interventions that may be used for selected patient populations (defined with recommendation).

All recommendations are considered appropriate.

pages.text:
Overview 

educational status, uninsured status, and non-white race to be associated 
with reduced access to HCT.3-6 Individuals from racially and ethnically 
diverse backgrounds are less likely to find an HLA-donor match, in part 
due to variations in HLA genotype frequencies between distinct human 
populations, as well as underrepresentation of donors from varied 
ancestries in registries.7 In addition to reduced access to HCT, studies 
have revealed that Black individuals have worse transplant-related 
outcomes, with significantly higher transplant-related mortality (TRM) 
compared to white individuals, even when controlling for insurance 
coverage.4 

Outcomes of HCT vary according to the type and stage of the disease 
being treated, the overall health and comorbidities of the patient, and for 
allogeneic HCT, the degree of HLA mismatch between donor and 
recipient, the source of the hematopoietic cells (see Graft Source) and the 
immunosuppressive regimen given to prevent graft-versus-host disease 
(GVHD), a common complication of allogeneic HCT.1,8 

Guidelines Update Methodology 

Hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) involves the infusion of 
hematopoietic cells after preparation with cytotoxic conditioning regimens 
in order to eradicate disease and establish adequate hematopoietic and 
immune function.1 HCT is potentially curative for patients with certain 
types of hematologic malignancies and is also used to support patients 
undergoing high-dose chemotherapy for the treatment of certain solid 
tumors. HCT is classified as autologous or allogeneic based on the origin 
of hematopoietic cells. An autologous HCT uses the patient’s own cells 
while an allogeneic HCT uses hematopoietic cells from a human leukocyte 
antigen (HLA)-compatible related or unrelated donor. Prior to HCT, most 
patients receive chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and/or radiation therapy 
for pre-transplant conditioning (conditioning regimen). In allogeneic HCT, 
conditioning regimens are administered in order to eradicate malignant 
cells in the bone marrow (if using a myeloablative [MA] regimen) and to 
immunosuppress the recipient so that engraftment of healthy donor cells 
can occur.1 In autologous HCT, MA conditioning regimens are used to 
treat the malignancy. This is followed by rescue infusion of the patient’s 
own cells, which are collected and stored before high-dose therapy, in 
order to restore hematopoiesis and reconstitute the immune system.1 

The complete details of the Development and Update of the NCCN 
Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology (NCCN Guidelines®) are available 
at www.NCCN.org. 

Literature Search Criteria 

The Center for International Blood and Marrow Transplant Research 
(CIBMTR) estimates a total of >21,000 allogeneic and autologous 
transplants were performed in the United States in 2024.2 Acute myeloid 
leukemia (AML), myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS)/myeloproliferative 
neoplasms (MPN), and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) were the most 
common malignancies treated with allogeneic HCT, while autologous HCT 
was used most frequently in multiple myeloma (MM)/plasma cell disorders, 
non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL), and Hodgkin lymphoma (HL).2 Difficult 
logistics and high costs create significant barriers to access for many 
patients. Studies have found older age, lower socioeconomic status, lower 

Prior to the update of the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines (NCCN 
Guidelines®) for Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation, an electronic search 
of the PubMed database was performed to obtain key literature in HCT 
published since the previous Guidelines update, using the following search 
terms: hematopoietic stem cell transplant; allogeneic cell transplant; 
autologous cell transplant; and graft-versus-host disease. The PubMed 
database was chosen as it remains the most widely used resource for 
medical literature and indexes peer-reviewed biomedical literature.9 

MS-2

pages.title: Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT)
pages.text:
Autologous Hematopoietic Cell Transplant 

The search results were narrowed by selecting studies in humans 
published in English. Results were confined to the following types: Clinical 
Trial, Phase II; Clinical Trial, Phase III; Clinical Trial, Phase IV; Guideline; 
Practice Guideline; Meta-Analysis; Randomized Controlled Trial; 
Systematic Reviews; and Validation Studies. 

The data from key PubMed articles as well as articles from additional 
sources deemed as relevant to these Guidelines as discussed by the 
Panel during the Guidelines update have been included in this version of 
the Discussion section. Recommendations for which high-level evidence is 
lacking are based on the Panel’s review of lower-level evidence and 
expert opinion. 

Sensitive/Inclusive Language Usage 

Autologous HCT is performed to replace or “rescue” hematopoietic cells 
damaged by the high-dose chemotherapy used to treat certain advanced 
or high-risk hematologic malignancies and solid tumors. Hematopoietic 
cells collected from the patient prior to receipt of high-dose chemotherapy 
are infused back into the patient after administration of the preparative 
regimen.1 High-dose chemotherapy with autologous HCT is an effective 
treatment for several hematologic malignancies, including MM,10-14 
relapsed/refractory (R/R) HL,15,16 and R/R NHL.17-19 While autologous HCT 
may prolong progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) for 
patients with MM, it is not curative.20 Autologous HCT is also used in 
patients receiving high-dose chemotherapy for the treatment of certain 
solid tumors, including testicular germ cell tumors21-24 and some central 
nervous system tumors,25-29 for whom hematologic toxicity would 
otherwise limit chemotherapy administration. Additionally, autologous HCT 
is sometimes used as consolidation therapy for certain patients with 
AML.30 

Since autologous HCT uses the patient’s own cells, these patients do not 
typically develop GVHD. Additionally, these patients often have a lower 
risk of infectious complications since they do not receive post-transplant 
immunosuppression. Compared to allogeneic HCT, autologous HCT is 
associated with less morbidity and mortality but greater risk of disease 
relapse.1 There is no benefit to graft purging (ex vivo manipulation to 
eliminate residual neoplastic cells) prior to autologous HCT. 31,32 

Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplant 

Allogeneic HCT is performed to replace malignant (or defective) 
hematopoietic cells using those from a healthy donor. A preparative 
regimen consisting of chemotherapy (often high-dose), immunotherapy, 
and/or total body (or lymphoid) irradiation is given prior to allogeneic HCT 

NCCN Guidelines strive to use language that advances the goals of 
equity, inclusion, and representation. NCCN Guidelines endeavor to use 
language that is person-first; not stigmatizing; anti-racist, anti-classist, 
anti-misogynist, anti-ageist, anti-ableist, and anti-weight-biased; and 
inclusive of individuals of all sexual orientations and gender identities. 
NCCN Guidelines incorporate non-gendered language, instead focusing 
on organ-specific recommendations. This language is both more accurate 
and more inclusive and can help fully address the needs of individuals of 
all sexual orientations and gender identities. NCCN Guidelines will 
continue to use the terms men, women, female, and male when citing 
statistics, recommendations, or data from organizations or sources that do 
not use inclusive terms. Most studies do not report how sex and gender 
data are collected and use these terms interchangeably or inconsistently. 
If sources do not differentiate gender from sex assigned at birth or organs 
present, the information is presumed to predominantly represent cisgender 
individuals. NCCN encourages researchers to collect more specific data in 
future studies and organizations to use more inclusive and accurate 
language in their future analyses.

pages.title: Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT)
pages.text:
Graft Source 

to eliminate residual malignant cells and to suppress the recipient’s 
immune system, which is necessary to allow for engraftment of the donor-
derived cells and to prevent graft rejection. 

Indications for Transplantation 

Indications for HCT (allogeneic or autologous) vary by disease type and 
remission status. Information on indications for HCT can be found in 
disease-specific NCCN Guidelines (available at www.NCCN.org). The 
American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy (ASTCT) has 
also published clinical practice guidelines on indications for autologous 
and allogeneic HCT.33 

Hematopoietic cells can be obtained from peripheral blood, bone marrow, 
or umbilical cord blood (UCB). Several clinical factors should be 
considered when determining the optimal graft source for an individual 
patient, including disease type, disease stage, patient comorbidities, and 
the urgency for transplantation.33 The use of peripheral blood progenitor 
cells (PBPCs) has largely replaced the use of bone marrow grafts (in 
particular for autologous HCT) due to the ease of collection, avoidance of 
general anesthesia, more rapid engraftment rates, and reduced risk of 
graft failure.46-48 However, allogeneic PBPC transplants are associated 
with an increased risk of chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD) 
compared to bone marrow transplants.48-50 Several investigators have 
advocated for the use of bone marrow grafts for haploidentical HCT and 
HLA-mismatched unrelated donor (MMUD) HCT to reduce the risk of 
GVHD.49-51 52,53 However, more recent studies using PBPCs in the setting 
of haploidentical and MMUD transplants with post-transplant 
cyclophosphamide (PTCy)-based GVHD prophylaxis indicate lower risks 
of acute and chronic GVHD, and improved GVHD- and relapse-free 
survival (GRFS) (see Donor Source).52,53 

UCB transplant was first reported to cure a child with Fanconi anemia,54 
and has been subsequently used successfully in patients with hematologic 
malignancies.55,56 Importantly, UCB provides a graft source for many 
patients who lack other donors, particularly for patients with mixed or non-
white genetic ancestry.57,58 

Allogeneic HCT improves outcomes in patients with many subtypes of 
AML34 and ALL,35 patients with MDS,36 patients with relapsed and/or 
refractory HL37 and NHL,38 and certain patients with chronic myeloid 
leukemia (CML),39 such as those with advanced-phase disease and those 
whose disease is refractory to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy, including 
patients with certain high-risk ABL kinase mutations. Allogeneic HCT has 
also been offered to some patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia 
(CLL),40 MM,41 and primary and secondary myelofibrosis,42 although 
benefits for these patients are less clear and toxicity may be greater. 
Decisions regarding allogeneic HCT are always complex and should be 
carefully weighed as part of shared decision-making between the 
transplant team and patient. Donor-derived immune cells may exert an 
immune-mediated cytotoxic effect against the recipient’s neoplastic cells 
(ie, graft-versus-tumor effect). This phenomenon was described several 
decades ago and its clinical impact was demonstrated in a seminal 
CIBMTR study of >2000 patients that showed a reduced relapse risk 
among patients with GVHD.43 The graft-versus-tumor effect is considered 
a major mechanism for sustained response following allogeneic HCT, in 
particular with reduced-intensity or non-MA (NMA) HCT.44,45 

Outcomes of UCB transplants have been comparable to HLA-matched 
transplants in some reports.59-63 Advantages of using UCB grafts include 
rapid cell procurement, lower incidence of cGVHD, and less stringent 
HLA-matching requirements; however, use of UCB is limited by the cell 
doses that can be achieved in recipients with higher body weights and is 
also associated with delayed engraftment, higher risk for graft failure, 

MS-4

pages.title: Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT)
pages.text:
higher rates of infectious complications, and higher costs for 
procurement.7,64 Therefore, UCB transplantation is typically reserved for 
patients without an HLA-matched donor and should be performed in 
centers with expertise in this procedure. 

Donor Source 

RIC/NMA conditioning were similar, with 1-year OS of 78.6%, with 8.6% of 
patients developing moderate/severe chronic GVHD at 1 year. In a phase 
III study among patients undergoing allogeneic HCT with PBPCs and RIC 
conditioning, including a cohort of patients with 7/8 MMUDs, patients were 
randomized to receive either standard GVHD prophylaxis with tacrolimus 
and methotrexate or experimental prophylaxis with PTCy, tacrolimus, and 
mycophenolate mofetil.70 GVHD prophylaxis with PTCy, tacrolimus, and 
mycophenolate mofetil was associated with improved 1-year GRFS 
(52.7% vs 34.9% with standard prophylaxis) and a lower incidence of 
severe aGVHD or cGVHD at one year. 

There are three potential donor sources for hematopoietic cells: related 
donor (family members), unrelated volunteers (from donor registries), and 
UCB units.1 HLA matching remains the most important factor when 
choosing a donor, although donor age is now recognized as a critical 
factor as well. An HLA-matched sibling remains the preferred donor 
source, although post-transplant survival is comparable among patients 
receiving hematopoietic cells from HLA-matched unrelated donors (MUDs) 
for several diseases.7,63,65 

Donor age is emerging as one of the most important predictors of 
outcomes in MUD and haploidentical donor HCTs.71-75 Retrospective data 
from 1802 patients from the CIBMTR suggest increased risk with donor 
age >30 years.74 Data revealed a significant 3-year OS benefit with a 
donor age of 18 years compared to a donor age of ≥34 years; however, 
there was minimal difference in OS with a donor age of 22 to 30 years 
compared to a donor age of 18 years.74 When using PTCy for GVHD 
prophylaxis, younger donors may be favored over HLA-matched donors in 
some scenarios.72,75 

The prospective BMT CTN 1702 trial utilized a MUD “search prognosis” 
strategy for donor selection, with the probability of finding an 8/8 MUD 
categorized as very likely if probability was >90%, less likely if 26%, and 
very unlikely if <10%.76 For patients who were less likely or very unlikely to 
have an 8/8 MUD, alternative donors, such as haploidentical donors, were 
more likely to be prioritized (P < .01). Similarly, for patients who were less 
likely or very unlikely to have an 8/8 MUD, alternative donors that were 
less preferential, such as MMUDs were more likely to be utilized (P < .01). 
All probability groups had comparable numbers of donors typed and time 
spent in donor typing. Of the 67% of patients in the entire cohort who 
proceeded to transplant, an 8/8 MUD was utilized for 94% of the patients 

Patients without an HLA-matched donor may also be candidates for HCT 
from UCB, as noted previously, or mismatched donors, which include 
haploidentical donors or MMUDs. A haploidentical donor is a first-degree 
relative who matches at least half of the HLA loci of the patient. Of note, a 
retrospective multicenter analysis found that use of haploidentical donors 
beyond first-degree relatives may negatively affect survival.66 While the 
high degree of HLA disparity that typically occurs with haploidentical or 
UCB donors has been associated with an increased risk of graft failure, 
haploidentical and UCB transplants have increased access to HCT for 
individuals with otherwise limited donor availability.7,59-63,67 Additionally, as 
noted previously, emerging data suggest that haploidentical and MMUD 
transplants with PTCy for GVHD prophylaxis yield comparable outcomes 
to HLA-matched HCT.52,53,68,69 A phase II trial assessed outcomes in 145 
patients undergoing allogeneic HCT with PBPCs, a MMUD, and GVHD 
PPx with PTCy, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate mofetil.52 Among patients 
who received MAC, 1-year OS was 83.8% and only 10.3% of patients had 
developed moderate/severe cGVHD. Outcomes for patients who received

pages.title: Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT)
pages.text:
Hematopoietic Cell Mobilization 

in the very likely probability group, while an alternative donor was used in 
91% of the patients in the very unlikely probability group. 

Pre-Transplant Recipient Evaluation 

Granulocyte-colony stimulating factors (G-CSF), including filgrastim, tbo-
filgrastim, pegfilgrastim, and filgrastim/pegfilgrastim biosimilars, are 
commonly administered in the HCT setting for mobilization of PBPCs. 
Mobilization of PBPCs by G-CSF has largely replaced use of bone marrow 
grafts due to the ease of collection, avoidance of general anesthesia, more 
rapid engraftment rates, and lower TRM.46-48 For donor evaluation and 
follow-up recommendations, refer to the FACT-JACIE International 
Standards, 8th edition; https://www.factglobal.org/ctstandards).90 

Hematopoietic Cell Mobilization for Autologous Donors 

Effective mobilization regimens for autologous donors include G-CSF plus 
plerixafor, G-CSF plus cyclophosphamide with or without plerixafor, 
granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) plus 
cyclophosphamide with or without plerixafor, pegfilgrastim plus plerixafor, 
G-CSF alone, G-CSF plus disease-specific chemotherapy with or without 
plerixafor, and G-CSF plus motixafortide (for patients with MM). Adequate 
PBPC collection depends on individual patient- and disease-related 
factors. The minimum target yield for PBPC collection is 2 to 5 x 106 
CD34+ cells/kg, with a target of 4 to 5 x 106 CD34+ cells/kg.91 Yields <2 x 
106 CD34+ cells/kg may result in delayed engraftment, while larger cell 
doses have been associated with a more rapid time to platelet and 
neutrophil recovery.91 

The pre-transplant recipient evaluation generates data to estimate the 
risks of relapse, non-relapse mortality (NRM), and OS. It also generates 
information that may inform other transplant-related decisions. 
Physiological age, as measured by performance/functional status and use 
of geriatric assessments, rather than chronological age, should be used to 
determine eligibility for HCT.33,77 Selected patients who are older with 
limited comorbidities and good functional status can safely receive HCT 
with a relatively low risk of NRM.78-81 Studies such as the recently 
completed BMT CTN 1704 are assessing the utility of geriatric 
assessment tools in predicting outcome of HCT in patients who are 
older.82 Determining functional status (Karnofsky or ECOG performance 
status) and HCT-Comorbidity Index (HCT-CI) score83 are essential to 
determine candidacy for HCT (in particular for allogeneic HCT). HCT-CI 
score has been validated to predict the risk of NRM and estimated survival 
after allogeneic transplant.84,85 HCT-CI has also been shown to predict 
survival after autologous transplant.86,87 Furthermore, an updated 
composite-age HCT-CI has also been shown to have the same utility.88 
Detailed clinical assessment of HCT-CI has been published.89 For specific 
information on pre-transplant donor evaluation and HLA typing, refer to the 
Foundation for the Accreditation of Cellular Therapy and Joint 
Accreditation Committee - International Society for Cell and Gene Therapy 
(ISCT) and European Society for Blood and Marrow Transplantation 
(EBMT) (JACIE) International Standards, 8th edition.90 For more 
information regarding pre-transplant recipient evaluation, see Pre-
Transplant Recipient Evaluation in the algorithm. 

Single-agent G-CSF (filgrastim, tbo-filgrastim, or filgrastim biosimilars) is 
effective in mobilizing PBPCs in the autologous setting.92-96 The addition of 
the CXCR4 inhibitor plerixafor to G-CSF mobilization accelerates the rise 
in PBPC count.97-105 In a phase III trial, the addition of plerixafor to G-CSF 
improved PBPC collection yields and reduced mobilization failure rates in 
patients with heavily pre-treated NHL, with 59% of patients in the G-CSF 
plus plerixafor group collecting ≥5 x 106 CD34+ cells/kg in ≤4 apheresis 

MS-6

pages.title: Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT)
pages.text:
the autologous setting. Chemomobilization regimens using other 
chemotherapy agents with disease-specific activity are also appropriate. 

Although there are limited high-quality data supporting the use of 
pegfilgrastim in this setting, some small studies suggest that pegfilgrastim 
may have similar efficacy to filgrastim for mobilization.110-115 Therefore, 
pegfilgrastim or pegfilgrastim biosimilars plus plerixafor are also 
appropriate options for mobilization in the autologous setting. 

Dosing and Administration 

days compared to 20% of patients in the G-CSF alone group (P < .001).103 
Another phase III trial found similar results in patients with MM, with 71.6% 
of patients in the plerixafor plus G-CSF group collecting ≥6 x 106 CD34+ 
cells/kg in ≤2 apheresis days compared to 34.4% of patients in the G-CSF 
alone group (P < .001).104 Therefore, G-CSF plus plerixafor as well as 
single-agent G-CSF are recommended for PBPC mobilization in the 
autologous setting. The addition of a novel cyclic-peptide CXCR4 inhibitor, 
motixafortide, to G-CSF may also improve PBPC collection yields in 
patients with MM, with 92.5% of patients in the motixafortide plus G-CSF 
group collecting ≥6 x 106 CD34+ cells/kg in ≤2 apheresis days compared 
to 26.2% of patients in the G-CSF alone group (P < .0001).106 Therefore, 
G-CSF plus motixafortide is a recommended PBPC mobilization option for 
patients with MM in the autologous setting. 

The NCCN Panel recommends administration of filgrastim, tbo-filgrastim, 
or a filgrastim biosimilar as single agents, or as part of a 
chemomobilization regimen for 4 to 5 days after the completion of 
cyclophosphamide (or other disease-directed therapy), at a dose of 10 
mcg/kg body weight per day in daily or twice-daily (split) dosing by 
subcutaneous injection. Sargramostim should be administered at a dose 
of 250 mcg/m2 per day either by intravenous infusion over 24 hours or by 
subcutaneous injection once daily for 4 to 5 days. Pegfilgrastim is given as 
a single dose of 6 mg by subcutaneous injection on day 1. Apheresis 
usually commences on the fourth or fifth day following initiation of growth 
factor. Plerixafor is generally administered by subcutaneous injection 11 
hours prior to hematopoietic cell collection. Plerixafor dosing is based on 
patient body weight and estimated creatinine clearance. Clinical judgment 
should be used when the white blood cell count is >50,000; these patients 
should be monitored carefully for splenic pain due to rare cases of 
splenomegaly or splenic rupture. 

Additional Therapy 

The addition of chemotherapy agents such as cyclophosphamide to G-
CSF may also result in higher PBPC collection yields with fewer days of 
apheresis compared to G-CSF alone and may reduce the burden of 
residual tumor.107,108 In a trial comparing chemotherapy + G-CSF to G-
CSF alone, the addition of chemotherapy resulted in higher total cells 
collected (18.6 x 106/kg vs 7.0 x 106/kg; P < .001), fewer days of apheresis 
(2.0 vs 2.9; P < .001), and fewer re-mobilizations (1.06 vs 1.2; P = .01) but 
also required substantially more apheresis days (12.5 vs 4.2 days; P < 
.001), with higher total cost ($19,614 vs $16,852; P = .003).108 In a study 
of patients with MM comparing cyclophosphamide plus G-CSF to 
plerixafor plus G-CSF, the cyclophosphamide group had significantly lower 
total CD34+ collection yields (median 7  x  106/kg vs 11.6  x  106/kg; P  = 
.001) and higher mobilization failure rates (8.1% vs 0), but significantly 
lower costs ($19,626.5 vs $28,980; P < .0001).97 Another study showed no 
difference in mobilization efficacy between G-CSF plus cyclophosphamide 
and GM-CSF (sargramostim) plus cyclophosphamide in patients with 
NHL.109 Therefore, G-CSF or GM-CSF plus cyclophosphamide with or 
without plerixafor are recommended regimens for PBPC mobilization in 

If CD34+ cell yield is inadequate (<2 x 106 CD34+ cells/kg), consider 
increasing G-CSF dose or changing dose schedule. If not administered 
prior to cell collection, the addition of plerixafor to G-CSF or chemotherapy 
plus G-CSF is also recommended. The addition of plerixafor as a 

MS-7

pages.title: Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT)
pages.text:
filgrastim biosimilars for the mobilization of PBPCs in healthy allogeneic 
donors, but cautions physicians to closely follow patients receiving tbo-
filgrastim or filgrastim biosimilars during the follow-up period in order to 
identify any potential complications or unexpected outcomes. The 
minimum target yield for PBPC collection in allogeneic donors is 4 to 5 x 
106 CD34+ cells/kg.91 

Dosing and Administration 

Single-agent filgrastim, tbo-filgrastim, or a filgrastim biosimilar should be 
administered at a dose of 10 mcg/kg per day in daily or twice daily (split) 
dosing by subcutaneous injection for 4 to 5 days. Apheresis usually 
commences on the fourth or fifth day following mobilization initiation. 

Additional Therapy 

preemptive (“just in time”) strategy in patients with poor mobilization after 
administration of G-CSF with or without chemotherapy has been highly 
successful.99,100,116-118 Risk factors associated with poor mobilization 
include older age, extensive prior therapy, prior radiation to marrow-
containing regions, low white blood cell count (<4000), or multiple cycles 
of certain agents such as fludarabine or lenalidomide.101,119-128 Additional 
studies have suggested there may also be genetic parameters that 
contribute to mobilization outcome.129 However, predicting mobilization 
failure based on baseline patient characteristics or risk factors has 
historically been highly inaccurate.101 Bone marrow harvest can also be 
considered in the setting of poor mobilization.130 For bone marrow harvest 
recommendations, refer to the National Marrow Donor Program/Be the 
Match. If feasible, consider rest for 2 to 4 weeks before a remobilization 
attempt. 

Hematopoietic Cell Mobilization for Allogeneic Donors 

If CD34+ cell yield is inadequate (<4 x 106 CD34+ cells/kg), consider 
addition of plerixafor to G-CSF. Bone marrow harvest is an alternative 
option.130 For bone marrow harvest recommendations, refer to the 
National Marrow Donor Program/Be the Match. 

Principles of Conditioning for HCT 

Conditioning for autologous transplant is based on disease and recipient 
age/comorbidities, while conditioning for allogeneic transplant is based on 
disease as well as recipient age/comorbidities, graft source, and degree of 
HLA disparity. 

Conditioning regimens are categorized into three groups based on their 
intensity: MA, NMA, or reduced-intensity conditioning (RIC).142 MA 
regimens cause irreversible (or near irreversible) pancytopenia. 
Hematopoietic cell support is required to rescue marrow function and 
prevent aplasia-related death. Regimens that include total body irradiation 
(TBI) (≥5 Gy single dose or ≥8 Gy fractionated) or busulfan >8 mg/kg 

G-CSF alone should be used to mobilize allogeneic donors. Initially, there 
were concerns about using G-CSF for mobilization in the allogeneic 
setting due to toxicity for the donor and the risk for GVHD in the recipient. 
However, studies have demonstrated filgrastim to be well-tolerated by 
donors without an effect on long-term survival in the recipient.131-133 Data 
supporting the use of filgrastim biosimilars in the allogeneic setting are 
sparse. Some studies have suggested that filgrastim biosimilars are 
effective for mobilization in healthy donors with no short-term safety 
issues,134-138 but long-term data are needed. In a study by the World 
Marrow Donor Association (WMDA), mobilization of CD34+ cells and 
incidence of treatment-related adverse events were found to be similar 
between filgrastim biosimilars and reference filgrastim in 1287 healthy 
volunteers,139 although the authors cite a lack of long-term follow-up for 
both. Tbo-filgrastim has also been shown to effectively mobilize PBPCs for 
allogeneic transplantation in healthy donors.96,140,141 Based on these data, 
the NCCN Panel endorses the use of filgrastim, tbo-filgrastim, and

recipient evaluation or upon review of pre-transplant organ testing, 
frailty/geriatric assessment, or other evaluation. The selection of 
conditioning regimen intensity depends on many factors including patient 
age (chronologic and physiologic),88 performance status, HCT-CI score,89 
disease type, remission status (including measurable residual disease), 
and history of prior HCT. In patients who are young and fit, MA regimens 
may be preferred for ALL, AML, CML, and MDS.146 See HCT-A 3 of 10, 
Principles of Conditioning for Hematopoietic Cell Transplant, Examples of 
Commonly Used Conditioning Regimens, in the algorithm for a non-
exhaustive list of MA regimens commonly used in autologous, allogeneic, 
and UCB transplants. 

For MA regimens utilizing busulfan, pharmacokinetic (PK) monitoring with 
therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is required for oral busulfan and is 
preferred for IV busulfan in centers with expertise and the capability of 
measuring busulfan PK in real time. In certain populations, use of busulfan 
TDM rather than traditional weight-based dosing has been associated with 
lower rates of graft rejection and hepatoxicity, as well as reduced risk of 
relapse.144 In a trial of 218 patients undergoing allogeneic HCT, patients 
were randomized to conditioning with fludarabine with either weight-based 
or PK-guided IV busulfan with an area under the curve (AUC) goal of 6000 
µM-min.145 Weight-based busulfan dosing was found to be associated with 
higher rates of relapse or treatment-related mortality; while PK-dosing was 
associated with improvements in both OS and PFS, particularly in patients 
with MDS or those with AML who had not achieved remission at the time 
of transplant. Optimal busulfan exposure targets for all conditioning 
regimens remain undefined due to the absence of prospective randomized 
trials; however, most recommendations fall within 60-100 mg x h/L as the 
proposed total AUC target. Of note, busulfan plasma exposure unit should 
now be reported as AUC in mg x h/L.143 

NMA conditioning regimens produce moderate-to-minimal cytopenia, and 
graft rejection or graft failure, if it occurs, would be followed by autologous 
hematopoietic recovery. Examples include TBI ≤2 Gy ± purine analog and 
total lymphoid irradiation + antithymocyte globulin (ATG). An RIC regimen 
is one that does not fulfill the criteria for either an MA or NMA regimen. 
RIC regimens differ from NMA regimens in that they cause cytopenias that 
do require hematopoietic cell support, but the doses of alkylating agents or 
TBI is reduced in comparison to MA regimens.142 

If UCB transplant is being used, referral to a center with experience in 
UCB transplants is strongly recommended. If an MA conditioning regimen 
is planned for a recipient of UCB, omidubicel-onlv, an ex vivo 
nicotinamide-modified allogeneic hematopoietic progenitor cell therapy 
derived from a single cord blood unit, has been shown to shorten the time 
to engraftment and reduce the risk of some infections.147 In a phase III 
trial, median time to neutrophil engraftment for UCB transplantation with 
omidubicel-onlv was 12 days compared to 22 days for standard UCB 
transplantation (P < .001).147 Similarly, platelet recovery was shorter in the 
omidubicel-onlv arm (55% vs 35% recovery at 42 days; P = .028). Grade 
2–3 bacterial or invasive fungal infections were also less common in the 
omidubicel-onlv arm (37% vs 57%; P = .027). An Expanded Access 
Program that assessed outcomes of patients with hematologic 
malignancies following UCB transplant with omidubicel-onlv found similar 
median times to neutrophil and platelet engraftment, at 12 days and 33.5 
days, respectively.148 The incidence of first grade 2-3 bacterial infections in 
the 100-day period post-transplant was 18%, while the incidence of first 
grade 3 viral infection in the first-year post-transplant was 12%. 

The choice among an MA, NMA, or RIC regimen is a nuanced decision 
that should be made by the transplant team at the time of pre-transplant 

MS-9

pages.text:
(TMA), especially if used with MA regimens.156-159 Importantly, an 
increased risk of GVHD has been associated with pre-transplant treatment 
with immune checkpoint inhibitors (pre- or post-HCT) and 
mogamulizumab.160-163 Therefore, the Panel recommends considering a 
minimum 8- to 12-week window between these treatments and the start of 
transplant conditioning if clinically feasible. 

Conditioning Regimens without Fludarabine 

There have been intermittent shortages of fludarabine, which is a 
component of many conditioning regimens.164 To address this, the Panel 
has developed recommendations for non-fludarabine RIC regimens for 
use during times of shortage (see Principles of Conditioning for 
Hematopoietic Cell Transplant: Conditioning Regimens Without 
Fludarabine in the algorithm for a noninclusive list).The Panel suggests 
that the choice of regimen should be based on institutional preference and 
experience due to the lack of comparative data with fludarabine-based 
regimens. 

NMA or RIC regimens may be preferred for patients undergoing allogeneic 
HCT for treatment of lymphoma (NHL or HL), CLL, and plasma cell 
disorders such as MM and plasma cell leukemia. NMA/RIC regimens may 
also be preferred for patients who have received a prior autologous HCT 
and patients who are not candidates for MA regimens. See HCT-A 3 of 10, 
Principles of Conditioning for Hematopoietic Cell Transplant, Examples of 
Commonly Used Conditioning Regimens, in the algorithm for a non-
exhaustive list of NMA regimens commonly used in allogeneic transplant 
and HCT-A 4 of 10, Principles of Conditioning for Hematopoietic Cell 
Transplant, Examples of Commonly Used Conditioning Regimens, in the 
algorithm for a non-exhaustive list of RIC regimens commonly used in 
allogeneic and UCB transplants. Conditioning regimens commonly used in 
autologous transplants are listed by disease type on HCT-A 6 of 10, 
Principles of Conditioning for Hematopoietic Cell Transplant, Examples of 
Commonly Used Conditioning Regimens, in the algorithm). Suggested 
dose modifications by weight for many of the drugs commonly used in 
conditioning regimens are given in the Principles of Conditioning for 
Hematopoietic Cell Transplant: Suggested Doses/Modifications by Weight 
section of the algorithm.149 

Some of the regimens recommended by the Panel are associated with 
certain adverse events. For example, a systemic inflammatory syndrome 
has been reported with the use of clofarabine-based regimens, although 
concomitant steroid use may mitigate this risk.165 Additionally, use of 
certain cladribine-based regimens may be associated with increased risk 
of graft failure.166-168 The pentostatin + busulfan + cyclophosphamide 
regimen was reported with primary immunodeficiency disorders using 
post-transplant cyclophosphamide169 and pentostatin + TBI 4 Gy was 
reported for second transplant after engraftment failure.170 

Principles of GVHD Prophylaxis

There are certain special situations that warrant more caution. For 
example, use of high-dose busulfan, carmustine, or high-dose TBI in 
patients with significant pulmonary dysfunction should be carefully 
considered due to the substantial additional risk to the lungs.150-152 The use 
of high-dose busulfan and high-dose TBI has been associated with an 
increased risk of sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) in patients with 
significant liver dysfunction.153 An increased risk of SOS has also been 
associated with the use of dual alkylator-based regimens with pre-
transplant inotuzumab or gemtuzumab.154 Additionally, the alkylating agent 
thiotepa can be excreted through the skin and requires special skin 
care.155 The combination of sirolimus and tacrolimus may also be 
associated with higher risk of SOS and thrombotic microangiopathy

Post-Transplant Follow-up 

>95% donor cells in both the myeloid and lymphoid compartment, mixed 
donor chimerism as anywhere from 5% to 95% donor cells, and anything 
<5% as the absence of donor chimerism.179 Studies have shown that 
decreased donor chimerism is associated with an increased risk of 
relapse in patients with acute leukemia and is a concern for other diseases 
as well.180,181 

Late complications (after the first 100 days) include infections; late 
radiation-related toxicities (eg, cataracts, hypothyroidism); late 
chemotherapy-related toxicities (eg, heart failure); organ dysfunction; 
secondary malignancies including therapy-related myeloid neoplasms, 
breast and thyroid cancers, melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancers; 
endocrinopathies; and infertility, among others.173,177 GVHD is a common 
and significant risk in allogeneic HCT recipients. In GVHD, donor 
lymphocytes recognize the recipient’s tissues as foreign, resulting in 
immune-mediated cellular injury. There is evidence that the humoral 
immune system is involved in the immunopathophysiology of GVHD as 
well, through B-cell antibody-mediated mechanisms as well as cytokine 
production.182 

Advances in HCT treatment paradigms, including supportive care, have 
led to improved survival.171 However, disease relapse and post-transplant 
complications continue to pose a major threat to HCT recipients. Disease 
relapse is more frequent in patients with advanced disease and in those 
receiving NMA conditioning regimens.172 Intensive supportive care is 
required for all post-transplant recipients until engraftment occurs. Post-
transplant complications are common after both allogeneic and autologous 
HCT and are often caused by the conditioning regimen,173,174 delayed 
immune reconstitution, and/or GVHD (for allogeneic HCT and very rarely 
autologous HCT). The risk and type of complications are also influenced 
by patient-related factors such as age, performance status, and 
comorbidities.65,175,176 Early complications (generally occurring within the 
first 100 days post-HCT) include prolonged cytopenia/delayed engraftment 
(also known as primary graft failure), graft rejection or secondary graft 
failure, infections, hepatic veno-occlusive disease (VOD)/SOS, and other 
organ toxicities such as cardiomyopathy or idiopathic pneumonia 
syndrome (IPS).173,177,178 Based on non-randomized trials, defibrotide is 
FDA approved for the treatment of hepatic VOD/SOS in patients with renal 
or pulmonary dysfunction following HCT (see defibrotide prescribing 
information for further details). 

Acute GVHD (aGVHD) typically manifests in the skin, gastrointestinal (GI) 
tract, and/or liver, while chronic GVHD may affect any organ but most 
commonly affects the eyes, mucosal surfaces, skin/joints/fascia, muscles, 
liver, and lungs. 

Common causes of NRM after allogeneic HCT include GVHD, infections, 
cardiovascular disease, secondary malignancies, and organ toxicity.183-186 
Common causes of NRM after autologous HCT include organ toxicity, 
cardiovascular disease, and infectious complications.187-189 Therefore, 
post-transplant care plans, including optimal supportive and survivorship 
care, are essential to optimize long-term outcomes in both autologous and 
allogeneic HCT recipients. 

Secondary graft failure occurs when cytopenias requiring blood products 
and/or growth factors develop following initial hematopoietic recovery.178 
Secondary graft failure can occur for a variety of reasons, including but not 
limited to inadequate cell dosing, immune-mediated events, and infection. 
Depending on institutional preference, strategies to monitor for or assess 
concern for secondary graft failure may include evaluating complete blood 
counts (CBCs), cellularity of the bone marrow, and donor chimerism.178 
Chimerism refers to the proportion of donor versus recipient cells present 
following allogeneic HCT, with complete donor chimerism defined as

Diagnosis and Grading 

Management of Graft-Versus-Host Disease 

GVHD is a common complication of allogeneic HCT and may be 
associated with significant morbidities and NRM.190-192 Despite advances 
in many aspects of allogeneic HCT, such as improved donor selection, 
more effective GVHD prophylaxis, increasing use of RIC, and ursodiol 
prophylaxis, GVHD remains a significant clinical problem. Mild 
manifestations of GVHD limited to a single organ are often managed with 
close observation, topical treatment, or by slowing tapering the 
immunosuppressive agents.193 More severe manifestations or multi-organ 
involvement typically require systemic corticosteroid treatment as the first-
line approach; the addition of secondary agents may be required for 
patients who do not experience response to initial steroid therapy or who 
are unable to taper or discontinue steroids.192 GVHD management can be 
optimized with coordinated care from a multidisciplinary team, preferably 
in medical centers with access to specialized transplant services. 

Acute Graft-Versus-Host Disease 

If aGVHD is suspected, organ-appropriate additional tests such as stool 
infectious disease testing, imaging studies, and/or viral testing should be 
performed to rule out non-GVHD causes of the symptoms. Organ-directed 
biopsies can then be performed as clinically indicated to support the 
presence of aGVHD or to exclude other diagnoses. GI biopsy (via 
esophagogastroduodenoscopy [EGD], colonoscopy, and/or flexible 
sigmoidoscopy) is recommended, whenever possible, for the diagnosis of 
GI aGVHD, particularly if stool infectious disease testing is unrevealing. 
Rectosigmoid biopsies were shown in one study to have higher sensitivity 
and negative predictive value than biopsies at other sites, whether the 
patient presented with diarrhea, nausea, or vomiting.197 Liver function tests 
(LFTs) should be routinely monitored after allogeneic HCT for early 
detection of hepatic aGVHD, which is often asymptomatic and can 
manifest with elevated transaminases without elevated bilirubin. Liver 
biopsy may be considered in patients presenting with unexplained 
abnormal LFTs without evidence of aGVHD elsewhere if the information 
would inform treatment. Once the diagnosis of aGVHD is made, the organ 
staging and overall grade of aGVHD should be determined to guide choice 
of therapy and disease monitoring. 

Up to 50% of allogeneic HCT recipients will develop aGVHD.184,194,195 Risk 
factors include degree of HLA-matching, donor type, graft source, and 
choice of GVHD prophylaxis, which are often inter-related, as well as use 
of TBI in conditioning.192 The skin, GI tract (upper and lower), and liver are 
the three organs primarily affected by aGVHD. Skin aGVHD is generally 
characterized by maculopapular rash. GI aGVHD generally presents with 
symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea. Liver aGVHD 
typically manifests with hyperbilirubinemia as well as elevated 
transaminases.194,196 Pathologic confirmation of aGVHD should be 
considered whenever possible, especially before initiating or escalating 
systemic immunosuppression. Although biopsies are not absolutely 
sensitive or pathognomonic, they may help exclude other diagnostic 
considerations. 

Following an aGVHD diagnosis, clinicians should remain attuned to the 
possibility of alternative diagnoses causing persistent or worsening 
symptoms. For example, persistent diarrhea in a patient with a history of 
GI aGVHD may be related to mucosal denudation with delayed healing 
due to compromised gut epithelial stem cell function, yet without active 
GVHD. On a case-by-case basis, repeat EGD/colonoscopy may therefore 
be indicated to differentiate which patients may benefit from additional 
immunosuppressive agents. Similarly, if one affected organ system has 
shown improvement with aGVHD management and another is worsening 
on therapy, an alternative explanation should be investigated, as it is 
unusual to have disparate responses in different organ systems.

topical steroids can be discontinued. Options for patients with no response 
to first-line therapy include enrollment in a well-designed clinical trial or 
continuing topical steroids (see GVHD Steroid Response 
Definitions/Criteria in the algorithm). Patients with progression and/or 
symptomatic rash (eg, pruritus, pain, sloughing, increasing BSA 
involvement) should be treated according to the recommendations for 
grade II–IV aGVHD. 

Grades II–IV 

The clinical grade of aGVHD is predictive of survival. Glucksberg aGVHD 
grading criteria were first proposed in 1974.198 Modified Glucksberg 
(consensus or Keystone) criteria were developed in 1994 (see Acute 
GVHD: Staging and Grading in the algorithm for modified Glucksberg 
grading criteria).190 The IBMTR Severity Index was subsequently 
developed,199 and was shown to be more predictive of HCT outcome when 
compared with the original Glucksberg criteria.200 Minnesota criteria have 
also been devised to identify patients with “high-risk” aGVHD who could 
benefit from early escalated therapy.201,202 More recently, MAGIC (Mount 
Sinai Acute GVHD International Consortium) criteria were developed (see 
Acute GVHD: Staging and Grading in the algorithm for MAGIC grading 
criteria).203 A joint task force of the EBMT, National Institutes of Health 
(NIH), and CIBMTR has published a position statement on standardized 
terminology for GVHD.204 Furthermore, blood biomarkers are being 
investigated for their utility as a predictive tool in aGVHD.205-208 

First-Line Therapy of aGVHD 

Grade I 

Grade I aGVHD affects only the skin (stage 1–2, <50% body surface area 
[BSA] non-bullous rash), with no GI or liver involvement.190 First-line 
therapy options for these patients include continuing (or restarting) the 
original immunosuppressive agent(s) and administering topical steroids 
(eg, triamcinolone, clobetasol) and/or topical tacrolimus. Medium- to high-
potency topical steroid formulations are recommended, except on the face 
or intertriginous areas where low-potency hydrocortisone is to be used (to 
avoid skin atrophy, telangiectasia, and acneiform eruptions). 
Antihistamines may be used for symptomatic relief of itching as needed. 
Alternatively, the patient can be observed without treatment if the rash is 
asymptomatic and stable. If there is a response to first-line therapy, as 
indicated by a resolution of the rash and associated symptoms, the 
immunosuppressive agent(s) should be tapered as clinically feasible and 

Enrollment in a well-designed clinical trial is encouraged for all patients 
presenting with grade II–IV aGVHD. The original immunosuppressive 
agent(s) may be restarted, continued, or escalated (with or without 
therapeutic drug monitoring) if aGVHD developed during tapering of 
immunosuppressive therapy; alternatively, additional agents may be 
initiated. Administration of systemic corticosteroids (± topical steroids) is 
the standard first-line treatment option (unless contraindicated or 
associated with severe intolerance) for patients with grades II–IV 
aGVHD.194,196,209 A phase III randomized controlled trial showed that initial 
treatment with low-dose systemic prednisone (0.5 mg/kg/day) in 
conjunction with GI topical steroids (beclomethasone dipropionate ± 
budesonide) was safe and effective for managing upper GI symptoms (ie, 
nausea, vomiting, anorexia) in patients with grade II aGVHD, with or 
without skin involvement (<50% BSA), with diarrhea volumes <1000 
mL/day.209 Of note, budesonide alone is less effective at treating the upper 
GI tract. In patients with higher grade aGVHD, use of low-dose prednisone 
was associated with an increased risk of requiring secondary 
immunosuppressive therapy, but with no difference in survival. Thus, 
patients with grade II aGVHD may be treated with 0.5–1 mg/kg/day of 
methylprednisone (or prednisone dose equivalent). Patients with higher 
grade aGVHD should be treated with higher doses of systemic steroids 
(1–2 mg/kg/day methylprednisolone or prednisone dose equivalent). There 
is no role for escalation of methylprednisolone above 2 mg/kg/day.210 The 

MS-13

pages.title: Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT)
pages.text:
simultaneous addition of other systemic agents in conjunction with 
systemic corticosteroids as first-line therapy for aGVHD should only be 
done in the context of a well-designed clinical trial. Patients on high-dose 
steroids require significant supportive care (see Supportive Care for All 
Patients with GVHD). 

Accordingly, a phase III, multicenter, double-blinded clinical trial (BMT 
CTN 0802) was initiated comparing the combination of methylprednisolone 
at 1.6 mg/kg per day (or prednisone dose equivalent) plus mycophenolate 
mofetil versus methylprednisolone plus placebo as first-line therapy for 
aGVHD.213 A futility rule for GVHD-free survival at day 56 was met at a 
planned interim analysis after 235 patients (of 372) were enrolled. 
Outcomes of both arms were equivalent in OS, 1-year incidence of 
cGVHD, and infection risk. Therefore, mycophenolate mofetil provided no 
benefit when added to corticosteroids as first-line therapy for aGVHD. 

If there is a response to first-line therapy, as indicated by a complete 
resolution of GVHD or improvement in at least one organ without 
progression in any other organ, steroids should be tapered as clinically 
feasible, as a standardized taper approach has yet to be defined. Options 
for patients with no response to first-line therapy include enrollment in a 
well-designed clinical trial214 or the addition of other systemic agent(s) to 
the corticosteroids, with steroid taper as clinically feasible. See Suggested 
Agents for Steroid-Refractory aGVHD below for more information. 

The randomized phase II BMT CTN 1501 trial compared sirolimus to 
prednisone as initial treatment in 122 patients with standard-risk aGVHD 
as defined by the Minnesota GVHD Risk Score and Ann Arbor (AA1/2) 
biomarker status.211 At day 28, the overall response rates (ORR) for 
sirolimus and prednisone were similar (65% vs 73%) and there were no 
differences in subsequent development of steroid-refractory aGVHD or 
any other key outcomes. Patients in the sirolimus group experienced less 
hyperglycemia and had reduced risk of infections but were at an increased 
risk for TMA as compared to patients in the prednisone group (10% vs 
1.6%). Thus, sirolimus can be considered as an alternative to systemic 
corticosteroids as first-line therapy for patients with standard-risk aGVHD, 
as defined by clinical risk score and, if available, Ann Arbor biomarker 
status. 

Chronic Graft-Versus-Host Disease 

Alternative regimens have been investigated as first-line therapy for 
aGVHD. BMT CTN 0302 was a randomized, 4-arm, phase II clinical trial (n 
= 180) that compared different agents (etanercept, mycophenolate mofetil, 
denileukin diftitox, and pentostatin) in combination with 
methylprednisolone at 2 mg/kg per day (or prednisone dose equivalent) for 
treatment of newly diagnosed aGVHD.212 The day 28 ORRs were: 
etanercept, 26%; mycophenolate mofetil, 60%; denileukin diftitox, 53%; 
and pentostatin, 38%. The corresponding 9-month OS rates were: 47%, 
64%, 49%, and 47%, respectively. Risk of severe infections were: 
etanercept, 48%; mycophenolate mofetil, 44%; denileukin, 62%; and 
pentostatin, 57%. These results indicated that mycophenolate mofetil plus 
corticosteroids could be a promising regimen for initial therapy of aGVHD. 

cGVHD is the leading cause of NRM after allogeneic HCT. cGVHD is a 
profound detriment to quality of life and is associated with significant costs 
and health care utilization.186,215-217 cGVHD usually develops within the first 
year after HCT, but it can occur years later.192 cGVHD may affect multiple 
organ systems, most commonly skin, oropharynx, ocular, musculoskeletal, 
and pulmonary, and is characterized by fibrosis, dryness, and ulceration of 
mucosal surfaces and variable clinical features resembling autoimmune 
disorders.218 The NIH Consensus Development Project has published 
detailed recommendations for the management of cGVHD including 
diagnosis, assessment of organ involvement, monitoring response to 
treatment, and supportive care interventions.193,219-222 A thorough 
understanding of the various clinical manifestations of cGVHD is essential 

MS-14

pages.text:
for the early recognition of signs and symptoms. Multidisciplinary care 
aimed at avoiding organ damage and preserving function is strongly 
recommended. 

Diagnosis and Grading 

continuing, or escalating the original immunosuppressive agent(s) and/or 
administration of systemic corticosteroids (0.5–1 mg/kg/day 
methylprednisolone or prednisone dose equivalent). The initial 
corticosteroid dose may vary depending on the organs involved, the 
severity of GVHD, and patient comorbidities. 

In lieu of systemic corticosteroids alone, sirolimus in combination with 
prednisone may be considered. A phase II/III randomized trial compared 
prednisone + sirolimus versus prednisone + sirolimus + a calcineurin 
inhibitor (CNI) in patients with newly diagnosed cGVHD (defined as those 
receiving <14 days of corticosteroids) or those with cGVHD that did not 
respond adequately to ≤16 weeks of initial therapy (prednisone and/or a 
CNI +/- an additional agent other than sirolimus).226 The addition of a CNI 
did not improve 6-month complete or partial response rates 
(48.6% vs 50.0%; P = .87), 2-year complete response (CR) (14.7% 
vs 15.5%; P = .90), and 2-year OS (81.5% vs 74%; P = .28) rates. There 
was a lower incidence of renal dysfunction on the prednisone + sirolimus 
arm. 

In all cases of suspected cGVHD, additional tests should be considered to 
rule out non-GVHD causes of the symptoms, such as infection, drug-
induced injury or toxicity, or malignancy. While a biopsy may be done to 
confirm the presence of cGVHD, this is not always feasible and is not 
mandatory if the patient has at least one of the diagnostic findings of 
cGVHD defined by the NIH Consensus Development Project (see Chronic 
GVHD: Diagnosis in the algorithm for diagnostic signs and symptoms of 
cGVHD).193 Manifestations of cGVHD include bronchiolitis obliterans 
syndrome (BOS), an inflammatory lung condition. Unless it is 
pathologically diagnosed (via lung biopsy), clinical characteristics of BOS 
(assessed by pulmonary function tests [PFTs] and inspiratory and 
expiratory CT imaging of the lungs) are only diagnostic of lung cGVHD if 
distinctive features of cGVHD are present in another organ (see Chronic 
GVHD: Diagnosis, GVHD-B 2 of 3 in the algorithm for the complete criteria 
required for diagnosis of BOS). cGVHD grading is done according to the 
NIH Consensus Development Project criteria (see Chronic GVHD: 
Grading in the algorithm).193 

There is emerging evidence that the use of certain plasma biomarkers, 
including but not limited to ST2, REG3α, and IL2RA, may provide 
prognostic information for patients with aGVHD.205,207,223-225 While there are 
insufficient data on utilizing biomarker panels to adjust therapy, they may 
provide helpful information on outcomes such as NRM. 

First-Line Therapy of cGVHD 

Topical steroids, such as triamcinolone or clobetasol, topical estrogen (for 
menopausal vaginal dryness and atrophy, which are often present and 
may complicate vulvovaginal cGVHD), topical tacrolimus, or 
dexamethasone oral rinse (for oral cGVHD) may be used as clinically 
indicated. Patients with lung involvement should receive inhaled steroids 
(eg, budesonide or FAM [fluticasone + montelukast + azithromycin]).227 
Azithromycin should be used only for the treatment of BOS and not for 
BOS prophylaxis due to possible increased risk for leukemic relapse and 
secondary neoplasms in patients undergoing HCT receiving azithromycin 
for BOS prophylaxis.228,229 Patients with progressive or worsening lung 
cGVHD following two to three lines of therapy may be evaluated for lung 
transplant. 

Enrollment in a well-designed clinical trial is encouraged for all patients 
presenting with cGVHD. Options for first-line therapy include restarting,
